title: Stopping a Signal Outside the Cell
endLine: Block a signal or receptor to test whether it is needed.

scenes.tts: A cell sits in a secreted signal and thrives, yet does it truly need that signal? To find out, block the signal outside the cell.
scenes.caption: A cell sits in a secreted signal and thrives, yet does it truly need that signal? To find out, block the signal outside the cell.
scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section of a tissue gap filling most of the frame height: on the left, a source cell releases glowing golden spheres labelled 'Signal' that drift across the gap; on the right, a target neuron displays matching cup-shaped receptors labelled 'Receptor'. As spheres dock, a bright pulse runs into the neuron and its branches extend. A bold question mark rises over the drifting spheres, then a translucent barrier ring highlights the open gap outside the cell. Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: A cell sits in a secreted signal and thrives, yet does it truly need that signal? To find out, block the signal outside the cell.

scenes.visual: Same schematic tissue gap with signal spheres continuing to drift gently in the background (no frozen frame). Title 'Stopping a Signal Outside the Cell' fades in cleanly at high contrast, then fades out.

scenes.tts: One tool is a neutralizing antibody, a protein built to bind one target. Added outside, it catches the free signal before it reaches the cell. The receptors stay empty, so the message inside fades.
scenes.caption: One tool is a neutralizing antibody, a protein built to bind one target. Added outside, it catches the free signal before it reaches the cell. The receptors stay empty, so the message inside fades.
scenes.visual: Same schematic tissue gap. Simple Y-shaped blockers labelled 'Antibody' (no molecular structures) enter the gap, latch onto the drifting golden signal spheres before they reach the right-hand membrane, and hold them in the fluid. The cup-shaped receptors on the target cell stay empty, and the glowing pulse inside the neuron dims. Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: One tool is a neutralizing antibody, a protein built to bind one target. Added outside, it catches the free signal before it reaches the cell. The receptors stay empty, so the message inside fades.

scenes.tts: A second tool is a decoy receptor, a free receptor fragment with no cell attached. Why does a receptor block signaling? Its binding pocket soaks up the free signal, leaving the cell's real receptors empty.
scenes.caption: A second tool is a decoy receptor, a free receptor fragment with no cell attached. Why does a receptor block signaling? Its binding pocket soaks up the free signal, leaving the cell's real receptors empty.
scenes.visual: Same schematic tissue gap. The Y-shaped antibodies drift out, and free-floating cup-shaped pieces labelled 'Decoy receptor'—identical in pocket shape to the membrane receptors but with no cell attached—enter the gap. Golden signal spheres dock into these floating cups instead of crossing to the membrane, so the cell's real receptors remain empty and the inner pulse stays dim. Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: A second tool is a decoy receptor, a free receptor fragment with no cell attached. Why does a receptor block signaling? Its binding pocket soaks up the free signal, leaving the cell's real receptors empty.

scenes.tts: You can also block the receptor itself. An antibody caps the pocket, or a short peptide plugs it from outside. Every blocker works the same way: keep signal and receptor apart, and watch what fails.
scenes.caption: You can also block the receptor itself. An antibody caps the pocket, or a short peptide plugs it from outside. Every blocker works the same way: keep signal and receptor apart, and watch what fails.
scenes.visual: Same schematic tissue gap. Decoy cups clear away and golden signal spheres drift back toward the membrane. On the upper membrane receptor, a Y-shaped antibody clamps directly across the cup mouth; on the lower membrane receptor, a short wedge-shaped 'Peptide' fits snugly inside the pocket so drifting signal spheres bounce away. A clear visual gap opens between the signals on the left and the blocked receptors on the right, while the neuron's branches retract slightly. Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: You can also block the receptor itself. An antibody caps the pocket, or a short peptide plugs it from outside. Every blocker works the same way: keep signal and receptor apart, and watch what fails.

scenes.tts: Test this with nerve growth factor, or N G F, which acts on sympathetic ganglia, clusters of nerve cells. A sample holds N G F and a second factor that opens eyelids early. You inject newborn mice with the sample plus antiserum, serum carrying antibodies against pure N G F. What happens to their ganglia and eyelids?
scenes.caption: Test this with nerve growth factor, or NGF, which acts on sympathetic ganglia, clusters of nerve cells. A sample holds NGF and a second factor that opens eyelids early. You inject newborn mice with the sample plus antiserum, serum carrying antibodies against pure NGF. What happens to their ganglia and eyelids?
scenes.visual: Same schematic gap, now holding two drifting sphere populations: golden spheres labelled 'NGF' and blue spheres labelled 'Second factor'. On the right, two simple readout icons stand next to the receptors: a cluster of neurons labelled 'Sympathetic ganglia' and a closed eye icon labelled 'Eyelids'. Y-shaped antibodies shaped specifically for golden NGF enter the gap, and the prompt 'Sympathetic ganglia? Eyelids?' appears in bold high-contrast text. Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Test this with nerve growth factor, or NGF, which acts on sympathetic ganglia, clusters of nerve cells. A sample holds NGF and a second factor that opens eyelids early. You inject newborn mice with the sample plus antiserum, serum carrying antibodies against pure NGF. What happens to their ganglia and eyelids?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause in the same schematic world: the prompt 'Sympathetic ganglia? Eyelids?' stays on screen while golden NGF spheres slowly bump into the Y-shaped antibodies and blue second-factor spheres drift freely toward the right. Gentle continuous motion, no answer revealed yet. Tag: 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The antiserum traps the sample's N G F and the mouse's own, so most sympathetic ganglia are destroyed. Cohen raised it; Levi-Montalcini and Booker saw this in newborn mice. Yet the eyelids still open early, because the second factor slips past untouched.
scenes.caption: The antiserum traps the sample's NGF and the mouse's own, so most sympathetic ganglia are destroyed. Cohen raised it; Levi-Montalcini and Booker saw this in newborn mice. Yet the eyelids still open early, because the second factor slips past untouched.
scenes.visual: Same schematic world resolves: the Y-shaped antibodies lock up the golden NGF spheres so NGF receptors stay empty, and the 'Sympathetic ganglia' cluster shrinks and fades with label 'Destroyed' (attribution tag 'Cohen; Levi-Montalcini & Booker'). Meanwhile, the blue second-factor spheres pass right by the NGF antibodies, dock on the lower receptor, and the 'Eyelids' icon opens early. Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The antiserum traps the sample's NGF and the mouse's own, so most sympathetic ganglia are destroyed. Cohen raised it; Levi-Montalcini and Booker saw this in newborn mice. Yet the eyelids still open early, because the second factor slips past untouched.

scenes.tts: A blocker can mislead if you miss dose or timing. The same antiserum has much less effect in older animals. Sensory neurons that need N G F are hit hardest earlier. In 1980, Johnson and colleagues destroyed rat sensory neurons with maternal antibody before birth. Test at the wrong age, and a real need looks absent.
scenes.caption: A blocker can mislead if you miss dose or timing. The same antiserum has much less effect in older animals. Sensory neurons that need NGF are hit hardest earlier. In 1980, Johnson and colleagues destroyed rat sensory neurons with maternal antibody before birth. Test at the wrong age, and a real need looks absent.
scenes.visual: Same schematic tissue gap with a horizontal developmental timeline scrubber added underneath ('Before birth' -> 'Newborn' -> 'Older', tagged 'schematic'). As the marker slides from 'Newborn' to 'Older', the same NGF antibodies enter the gap yet the sympathetic neuron cluster stays mostly intact. Sliding the marker back to 'Before birth', maternal antibodies enter and a separate 'Sensory neurons' cluster fades sharply ('Johnson and colleagues, 1980'). A glowing highlight brackets the active window.
scenes.narration: A blocker can mislead if you miss dose or timing. The same antiserum has much less effect in older animals. Sensory neurons that need NGF are hit hardest earlier. In 1980, Johnson and colleagues destroyed rat sensory neurons with maternal antibody before birth. Test at the wrong age, and a real need looks absent.

scenes.tts: Overlap can also hide a signal's role. When two receptors share a job, blocking one lets some signal through. So experimenters pair blocking with adding the factor, and check against genetics. In 2001, Fukuchi-Shimogori and Grove paired added F G F eight with a receptor-fragment blocker.
scenes.caption: Overlap can also hide a signal's role. When two receptors share a job, blocking one lets some signal through. So experimenters pair blocking with adding the factor, and check against genetics. In 2001, Fukuchi-Shimogori and Grove paired added FGF8 with a receptor-fragment blocker.
scenes.visual: Same schematic membrane, now carrying two overlapping receptor cups side by side. A blocker caps the first cup, yet golden spheres still dock into the second cup and send a partial pulse inside. The scene transforms into a paired-test schematic: left pulse adds 'FGF8' (gain), right pulse releases floating cup-shaped 'Receptor-fragment blocker' (loss), tagged 'Fukuchi-Shimogori & Grove, 2001'. A separate 'Genetics' checkmark appears off to the side as the general cross-check, not attached to that 2001 tag (Fukuchi-Shimogori and Grove used electroporation, not mutants). Tag: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Overlap can also hide a signal's role. When two receptors share a job, blocking one lets some signal through. So experimenters pair blocking with adding the factor, and check against genetics. In 2001, Fukuchi-Shimogori and Grove paired added FGF8 with a receptor-fragment blocker.

scenes.tts: With those checks, outside blockers unlocked discoveries. In 1984, Pierschbacher and Ruoslahti found R G D, fibronectin's cell-binding handle. Free R G D peptide fills the cell's grip site, so fewer cells hold on. In 1988, Caroni and Schwab's antibody I N one neutralized myelin proteins that block nerve growth. Its larger antigen was later cloned as Nogo A.
scenes.caption: With those checks, outside blockers unlocked discoveries. In 1984, Pierschbacher and Ruoslahti found RGD, fibronectin's cell-binding handle. Free RGD peptide fills the cell's grip site, so fewer cells hold on. In 1988, Caroni and Schwab's antibody IN-1 neutralized myelin proteins that block nerve growth. Its larger antigen was later cloned as Nogo-A.
scenes.visual: Same schematic cell membrane morphs through two concise discoveries (each tagged 'schematic', no molecular structures). First, a fibronectin strand's 'RGD' handle grips the cell's membrane receptors until free wedge-shaped 'RGD' peptides fill those receptor pockets and fewer cells stay attached ('Pierschbacher & Ruoslahti, 1984'). Second, dark myelin stop-signals halt a growing nerve branch until Y-shaped 'IN-1' antibodies neutralize them and the branch extends; the antigen is then labelled 'Nogo-A (cloned later)' ('Caroni & Schwab, 1988').
scenes.narration: With those checks, outside blockers unlocked discoveries. In 1984, Pierschbacher and Ruoslahti found RGD, fibronectin's cell-binding handle. Free RGD peptide fills the cell's grip site, so fewer cells hold on. In 1988, Caroni and Schwab's antibody IN-1 neutralized myelin proteins that block nerve growth. Its larger antigen was later cloned as Nogo-A.

scenes.tts: Ogawa, Mikoshiba and colleagues added antibody C R fifty to embryonic cortical cell cultures. Normal tissue then organized like tissue from reeler, a mutant mouse. In 1997, two groups together showed C R fifty recognizes Reelin, a secreted glycoprotein. Catch the signal or plug its receptor, and you test the need.
scenes.caption: Ogawa, Mikoshiba and colleagues added antibody CR-50 to embryonic cortical cell cultures. Normal tissue then organized like tissue from reeler, a mutant mouse. In 1997, two groups together showed CR-50 recognizes Reelin, a secreted glycoprotein. Catch the signal or plug its receptor, and you test the need.
scenes.visual: Same schematic extracellular gap opens onto a layered sheet of embryonic cortical cells in culture ('schematic'). Secreted spheres labelled 'Reelin' drift through the margin; when Y-shaped 'CR-50' antibodies trap them, the orderly layers scramble into the 'reeler' pattern (tag 'Ogawa, Mikoshiba and colleagues'). A small tag '1997: CR-50 recognizes Reelin' appears when that year is spoken. For the closing sentence, the frame smoothly returns to the clean single-gap motif: signal spheres caught on one side, a receptor plugged on the other, gently drifting.
